title: 19  Labs
section: 19.5 Lab 4 — Lean: Value Stream Mapping, Takt and Pull
text:
19.5 Lab 4 — Lean: Value Stream Mapping, Takt and Pull

You map the Précitech shaft line as it runs today, size it against customer demand, and redesign the flow. Working in draw.io (browser) you build a current-state value stream map; in Google Sheets you compute takt time, an operator balance chart and process cycle efficiency; and on AnyLogic Cloud (browser, free public tier) you compare push, pull and a kanban-capped supermarket. You finish with a future-state map carrying one SMED and one pull improvement. Everything runs in a browser — nothing to install.
AI use: permitted with disclosure, but not for the map itself or the takt / PCE calculations — those must be your own work. Name any tool you used and what for.


19.5.1 Learning outcomes

After this lab you should be able to:

Draw a current-state value stream map from a station data table, with a material-flow line, an information-flow line and a lead-time ladder.
Compute takt time from customer demand and compare it against station cycle times on an operator balance chart to find the bottleneck.
Classify observed waste against the seven wastes and compute process cycle efficiency (value-added time ÷ lead time).
Explain how push, pull and a kanban-capped supermarket differ in WIP and lead time, using simulation output as evidence.
Propose a future state and justify the projected lead-time reduction.




19.5.2 Prep work


Read Chapter 5 (Lean) on takt time, the seven wastes, pull systems, kanban and SMED, and the Chapter 3 material on line balancing.
Create a free draw.io document (app.diagrams.net — “Device” storage is fine, no account needed) and skim the built-in Value Stream shape library.
Confirm AnyLogic Cloud (cloud.anylogic.com) loads and that you can run a public model and edit its input parameters in the browser.
Download vsm_station_data.csv from FOL — the station table for the Précitech shaft line (cycle time, changeover, uptime, WIP, batch size per station).
Form teams of 2–3.




19.5.3 Materials & equipment


Computer with internet access; one per team is enough, one per student is better
draw.io (browser) — current- and future-state maps
Google Sheets (browser) — takt, balance chart, PCE
AnyLogic Cloud (browser, free public tier) — push/pull model
vsm_station_data.csv from FOL
The Précitech case study — demand is 250 kits/day on one 8-hour shift




19.5.4 Procedure

Run the setup step first: open vsm_station_data.csv in Google Sheets and read the column headings so you know what each station contributes.
Task 1 — Current-state value stream map (30 min). In draw.io, map the shaft line end to end: CNC turn → deburr → wash → inspect → the Lab 2 kitting cell → shipping. For each process box record cycle time (C/T), changeover time (C/O), uptime and batch size from the supplied table; put an inventory triangle with the WIP count between each pair of boxes; add the supplier and customer, the production-control box, and the information-flow arrows (forecast, daily order, schedule). Draw the lead-time ladder along the bottom — processing time on the lower step, inventory wait time (WIP ÷ daily demand) on the upper step — and total it to a production lead time and a value-added time. (3 marks)
Task 2 — Takt and the balance chart (20 min). In Sheets, compute takt time = available shift time ÷ customer demand for the 250 kits/day target (state your planned/unplanned downtime assumption). Build an operator balance chart — one bar per station, station C/T on the y-axis, a horizontal takt line across all bars. Name the bottleneck station and say by how much it exceeds takt. (2 marks)
Task 3 — Waste and process cycle efficiency (25 min). Walk the map and classify every wait, move and rework against the seven wastes (transport, inventory, motion, waiting, overproduction, overprocessing, defects) — at least one concrete example per waste that is present. Compute process cycle efficiency = value-added time ÷ production lead time from your Task 1 ladder, and state whether the line is “lean” by the usual 25 % rule of thumb. (2 marks)
Task 4 — Push vs pull on AnyLogic Cloud (25 min). Open the supplied push/pull model on AnyLogic Cloud. Run it three ways, changing only the control policy: (a) push — every station runs whenever it has parts; (b) pull — downstream withdrawal triggers upstream; (c) kanban-capped supermarket — a fixed WIP cap between the bottleneck and its predecessor. For each run record average WIP and average lead time from the model output, in a small Sheets table. (2 marks)
Task 5 — Future-state map (20 min). In draw.io, redraw the line with one SMED change (halve the changeover at one station and justify the halving) and one pull change (a supermarket or FIFO lane where you had push). Recompute the lead-time ladder and state the projected lead-time reduction and which of the seven wastes each change attacks. (1 mark)



19.5.5 Deliverables & submission

One team report (PDF) containing: the current-state VSM (draw.io export), the takt calculation and operator balance chart, the seven-wastes table and the PCE calculation, the push/pull/supermarket results table with a two-sentence interpretation, and the future-state VSM with its justification. If you used an AI tool for anything permitted, add a one-line disclosure. Submit on FOL by the end of the lab period.



19.5.6 Rubric

10 marks total.







Deliverable
Marks




Current-state VSM — process boxes with C/T, C/O, uptime, batch; WIP triangles; information flow; lead-time ladder totalled
3


Takt calculation correct (demand, shift time, downtime stated); operator balance chart vs takt; bottleneck named with the gap quantified
2


Seven-wastes classification with a concrete example each; PCE computed correctly from the ladder and interpreted
2


Push / pull / supermarket runs completed; WIP and lead time recorded for all three; interpretation consistent with the numbers
2


Future-state VSM with one SMED and one pull change; projected lead-time reduction justified against the ladder
1






19.5.7 Instructor notes


Prep: generate vsm_station_data.csv with Rscript R/make_lab_data.R and stage it on FOL. Publish the answer key from the same script — expected takt, bottleneck station, PCE and the push-vs-pull WIP/lead-time ordering.
Build or fork the AnyLogic Cloud push/pull model once and confirm the input parameters students need (control policy, WIP cap) are exposed on the public run screen. Test it through the college firewall the day before.
Confirm draw.io and cloud.anylogic.com are reachable on the lab network; both are on the Lab 4 / 13 firewall-check list in Teacher preparation.
Marking: the map and the takt/PCE arithmetic must be the students’ own (AI not permitted for those). Check the lead-time ladder actually totals to the numbers they quote — a ladder that does not add up is the most common error.
This is the takt reference for Lab 14 — students compare the RoboDK cycle time against the takt they compute here, so make sure the takt value is right.

title: 19  Labs
section: 19.6 Lab 5 — Ergonomics in Automated Manufacturing (REBA & Inseer)
text:
19.6 Lab 5 — Ergonomics in Automated Manufacturing (REBA & Inseer)

You assess three workplace tasks for musculoskeletal risk two ways: manually with the REBA (Rapid Entire Body Assessment) worksheet, and automatically with Inseer, an AI video-based ergonomic-assessment tool. You then compare the two methods.
AI use: permitted with disclosure. Note that Inseer is itself an AI tool and is required for this lab — that is a lab instrument, not a generative AI writing your report.


19.6.1 Learning outcomes

After this lab you should be able to:

Explain why ergonomics matters in an automated manufacturing facility and name common ergonomic risks and their effects on workers.
Score a task with the REBA worksheet and interpret the result.
Generate an ergonomic risk-assessment report with Inseer.
Compare manual vs. automated assessment — advantages and limitations of each.




19.6.2 Prep work


Review the introduction-to-ergonomics and REBA material (video links in the handout, Procedure topics 1–2).
Skim Cheatsheet - Egonomics -REBA.pdf and the REBA-worksheet.pdf.
Form groups of 3–4.




19.6.3 Materials & equipment


REBA Employee Assessment Worksheet (printed, one per student/group)
Inseer software tool — web-based; account/login required
Computer with internet access
Sample tasks from an automated manufacturing facility (videos / photo sets):

Task 1 — lifting boxes repeatedly
Task 2 — computer-workstation setup
Task 3 — floor cleaning with a buffer





19.6.4 Procedure


Intro to ergonomics — watch the overview videos (importance; common risks and impacts).
Overview of REBA — watch how to use the worksheet.
Task evaluation — each group is assigned one of the three tasks. Observe and analyse it, note ergonomic risks (repetitive motion, awkward posture, heavy lifting, vibration, glare, chair height …), score it with the REBA worksheet, and interpret the score.
Intro to Inseer — overview of the tool; input the task data and generate a risk-assessment report.
Data & observations — record REBA scores and Inseer results for the task; note insights.
Analysis — compare the manual REBA assessment with the Inseer report; discuss advantages and limitations of each.
Conclusion — reflect on the importance of ergonomics in automated manufacturing and the benefits of AI tools like Inseer.




19.6.5 Deliverables & submission

One group report containing: the procedure, your group’s REBA analysis, your group’s Inseer report, and your group’s observations and conclusions. Submit on FOL by the end of the lab period.

title: 19  Labs
section: 19.7 Lab 6 — SPC and Gauge R&R: the Virtual Caliper
text:
19.7 Lab 6 — SPC and Gauge R&R: the Virtual Caliper

Before you ask an LLM to do statistical process control in Python (that is Lab 8), you do it yourself, by hand, as the measurement system. This lab runs entirely inside this page: webR cells render a virtual vernier caliper at a hidden, seeded true value, you read the scale and type the value, and the readings you produce carry genuine human reading error against known ground truth — so bias, linearity, repeatability and reproducibility are all computable, which a paper Gauge R&R cannot do. You then build an X̄/R chart and compute Cpk against the Précitech shaft spec of Ø 25.000 ± 0.050 mm.
AI use: not permitted for the readings or the calculations — you are the measurement system being studied. You may use an LLM to check your written reflection only, with disclosure.


19.7.1 Learning outcomes

After this lab you should be able to:

Read a vernier scale to its resolution and record a blinded, randomised measurement set.
Run a range-method Gauge R&R: compute EV, AV, GRR, PV, TV, %GRR and the number of distinct categories (ndc), and judge gauge acceptability.
Estimate gauge bias and linearity against certified reference values.
Build an X̄/R control chart, apply the Western Electric rules, and compute Cpk against a two-sided specification.
Explain how an inadequate measurement system distorts a capability index.




19.7.2 Prep work


Read Chapter 10 (SPC — X̄/R charts, the Western Electric rules, Cpk) and Chapter 11 (MSA — bias, linearity, repeatability, reproducibility, the range method, ndc).
Skim the worked webR cells in Chapter 11: bias-calculation and range-method — you reuse that method here.
Nothing to install and no account to create. This lab needs no external service — if the book page loads, the lab works.
Form groups of exactly 3. Each group member is one of the three operators in the Gauge R&R study.




19.7.3 Materials & equipment


One computer per group with this book page open (a second screen helps — one person reads the caliper, one records)
The webR cells in this section (the caliper, the Gauge R&R calculator, the X̄/R + Cpk cell)
A spreadsheet or paper grid to hold 90 readings (10 parts × 3 operators × 3 trials) before you type them into the calculator cell
The Précitech case study: shaft blanks, AISI 4140, Ø 25.000 ± 0.050 mm




19.7.4 Procedure


webR runs top to bottom on one shared page environment. Run the setup cell first and leave it run; every later cell depends on the objects it creates. If a later cell errors with “object not found”, re-run the setup cell. Base R graphics only — do not add library(ggplot2); it is slow and fragile in webR and not needed here.

Task 1 — Calibrate your eye (10 min). Run the setup cell. Then run the demo cell three times with demo = 1, 2, 3; each prints the correct reading after you have written your own. The caliper resolution is 0.05 mm: read the last main-scale mark the vernier zero has passed, then find the vernier mark that best lines up with a main-scale mark and add that many hundredths. Zoom the browser if the coincidence is hard to see.
Task 2 — The measurement run (35 min). (2 marks) Each operator reads all 10 parts, 3 trials each, using draw_caliper(part, trial). Read blind — do not look at another operator’s numbers, and do not look at your own previous trial. Work through the parts in the randomised order the setup cell prints for you, a different order per operator. Record all 90 readings in your grid.
Task 3 — Range-method Gauge R&R (20 min). (3 marks) Type your 90 readings into the lab6-grr cell (10 parts × 3 operators × 3 trials) and run it. It reports EV, AV, GRR, PV, TV, %GRR and ndc by the AIAG average-and-range method — the same method as Chapter 11’s range-method cell, extended to 3 operators and 3 trials. Record every output.
Task 4 — Bias and linearity (15 min). (1 mark) Run the lab6-bias cell. It compares each operator’s mean reading of each part against that part’s certified reference value (printed by the setup cell), reports overall bias, and fits bias vs. size to get linearity. State the bias in mm and whether it changes across the size range.
Task 5 — X̄/R chart and Cpk (25 min). (3 marks) Run the lab6-spc cell. It generates a seeded 25-subgroup production dataset (5 shafts per subgroup) against Ø 25.000 ± 0.050 mm — the same for every group — draws the X̄ and R charts, and computes Cpk. On the printed chart: list every subgroup that breaks a Western Electric rule (one point beyond 3σ; 2 of 3 beyond 2σ; 4 of 5 beyond 1σ; 8 in a row on one side) and name the rule. Report Cpk and say whether the process clears the automotive Tier-1 bar of 1.33.
Task 6 — Reflection (15 min). (1 mark) Answer in a few sentences: (1) Is your gauge acceptable? Use the AIAG bands — %GRR < 10 % acceptable, 10–30 % marginal, > 30 % unacceptable; ndc ≥ 5 required. (2) Your %GRR came from a study on parts spanning the process range. If the measurement system contributes the %GRR you found, what does that do to the Cpk you computed in Task 5 — is the true capability better or worse than the number? (3) Would you release shafts to the customer on this gauge?

19.7.5 Deliverables & submission

One group submission (PDF or notebook export) containing: the 90-reading grid; the Gauge R&R cell output with EV, AV, GRR, PV, TV, %GRR and ndc; the bias and linearity output; the X̄/R chart with the Western Electric rule breaks listed and named, and the Cpk; and the Task 6 reflection. Submit on FOL by the end of the lab period.



19.7.6 Rubric

10 marks total.







Deliverable
Marks

19.7.7 Instructor notes


Prep: none beyond opening the rendered page and checking the webR cells load. This lab has no external dependency — no site, no account, no dataset file — which is deliberate: it removes the single-point-of-failure risk the browser labs otherwise carry (see Lab 1’s notes).
Run Rscript R/make_lab_data.R to print the Lab 6 answer key: the caliper_ref values, the expected overall bias (≈ +0.03 mm), and the expected %GRR / ndc / Cpk ranges. The caliper and SPC data are generated inside the webR cells, so there is no file to stage.
Groups must be exactly 3 — the study needs three operators. An absent member means the group runs 2 operators and notes it; do not let a group of 4 double up.
Marking: the readings must show real spread between trials and operators — a grid where every operator recorded identical values was not read blind. Check that %GRR and ndc are consistent with the EV/AV/PV they reported.
This lab is the “do it yourself first” half of the arc into Lab 8 (SPC in Python, directed by an LLM). Point that forward explicitly.

NoteThe course narrative — Précitech Components



You are a new process engineer at Précitech Components, a Tier-1 automotive supplier in Granby, Québec (the same plant documented in Labs 2–3). The plant runs CNC turning cells producing transmission shaft blanks for a major OEM customer; your cell produces roughly 250 parts per day.
Your plant manager, Sophie Tran, has seen what GE and Toyota are doing with predictive maintenance and wants to know whether Précitech can benefit too — without leaking IP to public tools, without trusting unverified outputs, and without a million-dollar infrastructure investment. She has assigned you to:

Learn enough about AI tools to use them safely and productively for daily engineering work (Weeks 1–2).
Build a proof-of-concept predictive-maintenance system using publicly available data and free tools (Weeks 3–5).
Present your findings and the deployed application to plant leadership (Week 6).

By the end of Week 5 you will have a working web application at a public URL. It will not yet work on Précitech’s actual machines — you used a NASA simulation dataset, not plant data — but it will demonstrate the methodology, code quality and user interface well enough for the plant manager to decide on next steps.

title: 19  Labs
section: 19.9 Lab 7 — Machine Learning, Week 1: AI Literacy and Prompt Engineering
text:
19.9 Lab 7 — Machine Learning, Week 1: AI Literacy and Prompt Engineering

The first lab of the machine-learning module, in course week 7 (the midterm is written in lecture time that week, so this lab period runs as normal). You compare how an LLM responds to poorly vs. well-structured prompts, deliberately trigger and document a hallucination, and use an LLM to generate the Python code you will build on in Lab 8. Set in the Précitech narrative above.
AI use: required — you are assessed on directing an LLM well, not on writing Python.


19.9.1 Learning outcomes


How an LLM responds to poorly structured vs. well-structured prompts.
How to detect and document an LLM hallucination.
How to generate Python code using an LLM and evaluate whether the output is trustworthy.




19.9.2 Prep work


Read Chapter Chapter 13, Week 1 (the AI landscape; how LLMs work; why they fail; IP risk; the R-C-T-C-F prompt pattern).
Create a free account on Claude.ai or chat.openai.com (free tier is fine).
Create a text file prompts.md in your course folder — you add to it throughout the session and submit it at the end.




19.9.3 Materials & equipment


Computer with internet access — one per student (individual lab)
An LLM chat account (Claude.ai or ChatGPT, free tier)
prompts.md (you create it)
No dataset or local install needed this week




19.9.4 Procedure

Exercise 1 — Bad prompt → good prompt (30 min). Five real prompts from manufacturing engineers, all of which produced poor results:








#
Original prompt
Why it fails




1
“explain SPC”
No audience, no purpose, no format


2
“what’s wrong with my process”
No context — the LLM will guess


3
“write code to plot data”
Which language? what data? what plot?


4
“is 1.33 a good Cpk”
The answer depends on the industry — the LLM needs that context


5
“summarize this FMEA” (then paste 30 pages)
No audience, no focus, no length cap



Rewrite each using the R-C-T-C-F pattern (Role, Context, Task, Constraints, Format), run the original and your rewrite, and compare. In prompts.md record: the original; your R-C-T-C-F rewrite (label R=, C=, T=, C=, F=); a two-sentence reflection on what changed.
Exercise 2 — FMEA summarisation at three audiences (25 min). Using the CNC Cell 3 FMEA in Chapter Chapter 13 (Week 1), craft and run three prompts that summarise it for (a) plant manager Sophie Tran — top business risks in one paragraph; (b) a quality engineer — top 5 risks by RPN with mitigation status; (c) a new operator — a plain-language “what to watch for” checklist. Compare the three outputs with a partner. Add the three prompts and a two-sentence reflection to prompts.md.
Exercise 3 — The hallucination hunt (20 min). Deliberately get the LLM to fabricate something and then verify it is fabricated — e.g. ask about a made-up ASTM standard number, made-up paper authors, or a made-up alloy. When it answers confidently, record in prompts.md: the exact prompt; the exact response (copy-paste); how you verified it was false; one sentence on how you would prevent this in your own workflow.






Warning



After you have personally caught an LLM confidently fabricating a citation, you will be far more careful about verifying LLM outputs in professional work. This one behaviour change is worth the entire week.


Exercise 4 — LLM-assisted Python starter code (30 min). Use the LLM to generate Python that, on a file spc_data.csv with columns timestamp, operator, part_id, diameter_mm, surface_roughness_um, cycle_time_sec, tool_age_cycles: loads the CSV and parses timestamp as datetime; plots diameter_mm over time with title and axis labels; prints the mean and standard deviation of diameter_mm; flags rows more than 3 σ from the mean; and does not crash on missing values. Constrain the prompt: pandas + matplotlib only; a comment above each logical block; runnable in Google Colab with no local paths; standard Colab libraries only. Read every line and make sure you can explain it — the instructor will ask in Lab 8. Save it as spc_starter.py.



19.9.5 Deliverables & submission

Submit via FOL by end of session:

prompts.md — before/after prompt pairs (Exercises 1–2) and the hallucination documentation (Exercise 3)
spc_starter.py — the Python code from Exercise 4




19.9.6 Rubric

10 marks total.







Criterion
Marks




prompts.md — five prompts rewritten with all five R-C-T-C-F elements present
3


FMEA summarised at three audiences — audience-appropriate and technically accurate
2


Hallucination hunt — a fabrication documented, with evidence of how it was verified
3


spc_starter.py runs, is commented, and the student can explain it on request
2






19.9.7 Instructor notes


Prep: confirm Claude.ai / ChatGPT and colab.research.google.com are reachable on the lab network. Post the FMEA table (Chapter Chapter 13, Week 1) and a blank prompts.md on FOL.
No dataset needed this week; spc_data.csv is staged for Lab 8.
Marking: Exercise 3 is the point of the week — require genuine verification (a screenshot of the empty ASTM search, a Google Scholar “no results”), not just “I think this is made up”.
The capstone (Labs 9–12) is assessed together against the capstone rubric in Lab 12; weights live in FOL and the instructor handbook, not here.

title: 19  Labs
section: 19.10 Lab 8 — Machine Learning, Week 2: Manufacturing Data and SPC
text:
19.10 Lab 8 — Machine Learning, Week 2: Manufacturing Data and SPC

You run your Lab 7 Python on real (messy) plant data — 90 days of production from Précitech CNC Cell 3, with intentional data-quality problems embedded — find and document each problem without silently deleting data, then build an X-bar control chart and compute Cpk. This is the SPC you did by hand in Lab 6, now directed through an LLM.
AI use: required — you direct an LLM to write the Python and must be able to explain every line.


19.10.1 Learning outcomes


How LLM-generated code behaves on real, messy industrial data.
How to find and document data-quality problems without silent data deletion.
How to build an X-bar control chart in Python and identify out-of-control events.




19.10.2 Prep work


Read Chapter Chapter 13, Week 2 (where plant data comes from; why industrial data is messy; statistical process control; where SPC fails).
Have your spc_starter.py from Lab 7 ready.
Open Google Colab and check you can upload files.




19.10.3 Materials & equipment


Computer with internet access; Google Colab
spc_data.csv (90 days of CNC Cell 3 data, with embedded problems) — from FOL
week2_lab.ipynb — pre-structured lab notebook, from FOL
Your spc_starter.py from Lab 7




19.10.4 Procedure

Task 1 — Run your Week 1 code on real data (25 min). Paste spc_starter.py into the first cell of week2_lab.ipynb and run it. Expect: a spike so large it compresses the chart; your 3 σ detector flagging the wrong rows; possibly a warning. In the first markdown cell, describe the spike (approximate value), whether outlier detection worked, and any error encountered.
Task 2 — Find and fix data-quality issues (35 min). Every change must be recorded in a quality-log DataFrame or markdown cell — never silently delete data (ISO 9001 traceability). Log pattern:
# Pattern for quality logging — add one row per correction
quality_log = []
quality_log.append({
    "row_index": 42,
    "column":    "diameter_mm",
    "original":  250.123,
    "corrected": 25.0123,
    "reason":    "Missing decimal point — impossible on Mazak QT-200 (max bar stock 51 mm)",
    "action":    "Divided by 10; rechecked against neighbouring rows",
})
Problems to find: two missing days (timestamp gap — document as a network outage, do not interpolate); one impossible diameter (> 30 mm — decimal correction); a block of rows with roughness in inches not µm (convert: × 25 400); one negative cycle time (flag and remove); and a real special-cause cluster around days 43–47 (keep it — document that it is a genuine event). After cleaning, verify no diameters > 30 mm remain, no negative cycle times remain, and the quality log is populated.
Task 3 — Build an X-bar control chart (35 min). Using the cleaned data, build an X-bar chart for diameter_mm (subgroup = 5 parts/day). Control limits use sigma / sqrt(n), not the standard deviation of the daily means. Spec limits USL = 25.050, LSL = 24.950. Identify which days are out of control, cross- reference them with the operator and tool_age_cycles columns, and compute Cpk using Equation 13.4 from Chapter Chapter 13:
mu    = df_clean["diameter_mm"].mean()
sigma = df_clean["diameter_mm"].std()
cpk   = min((usl - mu) / (3 * sigma), (mu - lsl) / (3 * sigma))
print(f"Cpk = {cpk:.3f}")
Expected: Cpk ≈ 1.1–1.2 (marginal — below the automotive Tier-1 standard of 1.33), with the out-of-control excursion around days 43–47.
Task 4 — Reflection (15 min). In a markdown cell, answer briefly: (1) how many parts had already been made during the days 43–47 event before the first out-of-control point appeared? (2) would a model predicting tomorrow’s mean diameter from today’s tool age, operator and the last 5 days of data have given earlier warning than SPC? (3) what data, not in this CSV, would you want to build a predictive rather than reactive model?



19.10.5 Deliverables & submission

Submit your completed week2_lab.ipynb (all cells executed, quality log populated, chart generated, Cpk computed, reflection answered) via FOL by end of session.



19.10.6 Rubric

10 marks total.







Criterion
Marks




Week 1 code runs against the real dataset
1


All five data-quality issues found; quality_log complete (row_index, column, original, corrected, reason, action); the days 43–47 special cause correctly kept, not deleted
4


X-bar chart with correct control limits — sigma / sqrt(n), not the std of daily means
3


Cpk against USL 25.050 / LSL 24.950, in the expected 1.1–1.2 range and interpreted
1


Reflection
1






19.10.7 Instructor notes


Prep: stage spc_data.csv and week2_lab.ipynb on FOL. Keep a key of the embedded problems (row indices, correct fixes) for marking.
The most common error is using the standard deviation of the daily means for the control limits instead of sigma_individual / sqrt(n) — check this explicitly.
Follow up on a spc_starter.py line from Lab 7: ask a student to explain it.
Marking: deduct for silent row deletion even if the final chart looks right — the traceable quality log is the learning objective.

title: 19  Labs
section: 19.11 Lab 9 — Machine Learning, Week 3: The C-MAPSS Dataset
text:
19.11 Lab 9 — Machine Learning, Week 3: The C-MAPSS Dataset

The capstone kickoff. You load NASA’s C-MAPSS turbofan run-to-failure data, compute the supervised-learning label (Remaining Useful Life, RUL) from the raw records, and identify which of the 21 sensors actually carry predictive information.
AI use: required — you direct an LLM to write the Python and must be able to explain every line.


19.11.1 Learning outcomes


How to load and explore industrial time-series run-to-failure data.
How to compute a supervised-learning label (RUL) from raw run-to-failure records.
How to identify which sensors carry predictive information.




19.11.2 Prep work


Read Chapter Chapter 13, Week 3 (the economics of maintenance; the P-F curve; the C-MAPSS dataset; the ML problem; the fatal mistake of row-wise splitting; Random Forest intuition; evaluation).
Get train_FD001.txt from the instructor’s FOL folder (or the Kaggle mirror, free account).
Open Google Colab.




19.11.3 Materials & equipment


Computer with internet access; Google Colab
train_FD001.txt — NASA C-MAPSS FD001 training set, from FOL
predictive_maintenance.ipynb — capstone notebook, pre-structured with starter code for Weeks 3–5, from FOL




19.11.4 Procedure

Task 1 — Load and label the data (20 min). The file has no headers and is space-separated: 26 columns = unit number, time in cycles, 3 operating settings, 21 sensors, and 2 trailing empty columns to drop. Expected: 20 631 rows, 100 engines. Then create the RUL label — there is no RUL column, you compute it:
# For each engine, the max cycle is the failure cycle
max_cycles = train.groupby("unit_number")["time_in_cycles"].max()
# RUL at any row = that engine's failure cycle minus the current cycle
train["RUL"] = train["unit_number"].map(max_cycles) - train["time_in_cycles"]
Task 2 — Visualise one engine’s life (30 min). Plot all 21 sensors for engine #1 over its whole life (a 7×3 grid). Classify sensors as flat lines (never change — useless), noise without trend, or clear trends (drift systematically toward failure — these are the useful ones). Write your lists in a markdown cell and compare with a classmate.
Task 3 — Identify constant sensors (20 min). Compute each sensor’s standard deviation across the whole dataset; sensors with std < 0.001 are effectively constant and carry no information. Expected: about 6 constant sensors in FD001 (sensor_1, 5, 10, 16, 18, 19).

Before deleting a near-constant sensor in a real plant: what would you investigate first, and what are three possible reasons a sensor might read constant? Are all three equally acceptable to engineering leadership?

Task 4 — Correlation with RUL (20 min). For the non-constant sensors, compute the Pearson correlation between each sensor and RUL; |r| > 0.5 marks the most predictive raw features. Expected top sensors: sensor_11 (r ≈ −0.71), sensor_4 (≈ −0.69), sensor_12 (≈ +0.67), sensor_7 (≈ +0.66).
Task 5 — Reflection (15 min). In a markdown cell: (1) if you plot RUL for all 20 631 rows in order, what shape appears and why — and what does that shape say about the danger of splitting rows randomly between train and validation? (2) which 3 sensors would you most want in a model, citing evidence from Task 2 or 4? (3) what would you do before dropping the 6 dead sensors in a real plant?



19.11.5 Deliverables & submission

Submit predictive_maintenance.ipynb with all four code tasks executed, the 7×3 sensor plot included, and the reflection answers written. Export as .ipynb and submit via FOL by end of session.



19.11.6 Rubric

Weeks 3–6 (Labs 9–12) are assessed together against the capstone rubric in Lab 12. For this session the instructor confirms progress: data loaded and labelled, sensor plot produced, constant sensors identified, correlations computed, reflection answered.



19.11.7 Instructor notes


Prep: stage train_FD001.txt and predictive_maintenance.ipynb on FOL (host the dataset yourself so it does not depend on Kaggle sign-in during the lab). Confirm Colab is reachable.
The “sawtooth” reflection question (Task 5.1) sets up the engine-wise split in Lab 10 — make sure students actually answer it.
Marking: rolled into the capstone rubric; here just verify the notebook runs end to end and the reflection is attempted.

title: 19  Labs
section: 19.12 Lab 10 — Machine Learning, Week 4: Building the Predictive-Maintenance Model
text:
19.12 Lab 10 — Machine Learning, Week 4: Building the Predictive-Maintenance Model

The capstone build. You engineer rolling-window features per engine, perform a correct engine-wise train/validation split, train a Random Forest to predict RUL, evaluate it against a naive baseline, and save the model for deployment.
AI use: required — you direct an LLM to write the Python and must be able to explain every line.


19.12.1 Learning outcomes


How to engineer rolling-window features per engine without data leakage.
How to perform a correct engine-wise train/validation split and verify it is clean.
How to train, evaluate and compare a Random Forest against a naive baseline.
How to save a trained model for deployment.




19.12.2 Prep work


Read Chapter Chapter 13, Week 4 (feature engineering for time-series; Random Forest internals; evaluation done right).
Have your predictive_maintenance.ipynb from Lab 9 with the data loaded, RUL computed, and the useful-sensor list established.




19.12.3 Materials & equipment


Computer with internet access; Google Colab
Your predictive_maintenance.ipynb from Lab 9 (continue in the same notebook)
Python packages available in a standard Colab environment (pandas, numpy, scikit-learn, matplotlib, joblib)




19.12.4 Procedure

Task 1 — Rolling features (25 min). For each useful sensor, compute a rolling mean and rolling standard deviation over a 5-cycle window, grouped by engine so the window resets at each engine boundary. Verify the boundary: engine #2’s first-cycle rolling mean must equal its raw value and must not include any of engine #1’s data.
Task 2 — Clip RUL at 125 (10 min). train_fe["RUL_clipped"] = train_fe["RUL"].clip(upper=125) — anything above 125 cycles is “basically healthy”. Plot the before/after histogram.
Task 3 — Engine-wise train/validation split (15 min). Hold out 20 engines for validation. Do not split rows randomly. End with an assert that must pass before you train:
overlap = set(train_data["unit_number"]) & set(val_data["unit_number"])
assert len(overlap) == 0, f"DATA LEAK: engines in both splits: {overlap}"
Build X_train / y_train / X_val / y_val, excluding non-feature columns (unit_number, time_in_cycles, RUL, RUL_clipped, the constant sensors, and the mostly-constant op_setting_*).
Task 4 — Train the Random Forest (20 min). RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=100, max_depth=10, n_jobs=-1, random_state=42); model.fit(X_train, y_train). Training takes 30–90 s in Colab.
Task 5 — Evaluate against the naive baseline (20 min). Compute validation RMSE and MAE. Compare with a naive baseline that predicts y_train.mean() for every row. Target: RMSE ≈ 20–25 cycles, at least 2× better than naive. If RMSE is suspiciously low (< 10 cycles) you almost certainly have a data leak — go back to Task 3. Produce a predicted-vs-actual scatter plot and describe the pattern (are predictions pulled toward the centre? more error at high or low RUL?).
Task 6 — Feature importance (15 min). Plot the top 15 features by mean-decrease-in-impurity. In a markdown cell compare with your Week 3 correlation analysis: are the top features raw or rolling? do they match the top-correlation sensors? what might explain a feature you expected but do not see?
Task 7 — Save the model (15 min). Save both files — the app needs the feature names and order:
import joblib
joblib.dump(model,        "rul_model.pkl")
joblib.dump(feature_cols, "feature_cols.pkl")
Download both from the Colab file browser; you need them in your GitHub repo for Lab 11.



19.12.5 Deliverables & submission

Submit via FOL: your completed predictive_maintenance.ipynb with all cells executed, plus rul_model.pkl and feature_cols.pkl (uploaded as files, or confirmed already in your GitHub repo).



19.12.6 Rubric

Assessed against the capstone rubric in Lab 12 (Working Predictive Model, 30 points; Code Quality, 20 points). The single biggest scoring risk is using scikit-learn’s train_test_split instead of a manual engine-wise split — the symptom is an RMSE of 5–8 cycles. If that happened, fix it: understanding and correcting the mistake matters more than a misleading score.



19.12.7 Instructor notes


Prep: none beyond Lab 9 — same notebook, same data. Have a reference solution notebook with the expected RMSE (~21 cycles) and feature-importance chart.
The teaching moment: circulate during Task 5 and look for RMSE < 10 — that is the row-wise-split data leak. Make students diagnose it themselves via the Task 3 assert.
Marking: rolled into the capstone rubric.

title: 19  Labs
section: 19.13 Lab 11 — Machine Learning, Week 5: Deploying the App
text:
19.13 Lab 11 — Machine Learning, Week 5: Deploying the App

You wrap the trained model in a Streamlit web application, push it to GitHub, and deploy it to Streamlit Community Cloud so it is live at a public URL — the proof-of-concept deliverable for Sophie Tran. Lab 14 (the take-home RoboDK work cell) is released this week — read its brief now so you can plan the build.
AI use: required — you direct an LLM to write the Python and must be able to explain every line.


19.13.1 Learning outcomes


How to wrap a trained ML model in a user-facing web application.
How to deploy that application to the public internet for free.
The difference between “works on my machine” and “deployed and accessible to others”.




19.13.2 Prep work


Read Chapter Chapter 13, Week 5 (the OT/IT boundary; dashboards and operators; model drift and the production AI lifecycle).
Create a free GitHub account and a new public repo named rul-predictor.
Create a Streamlit Community Cloud account at share.streamlit.io using your GitHub login.
Have rul_model.pkl and feature_cols.pkl from Lab 10 on your machine.




19.13.3 Materials & equipment


Computer with internet access
GitHub account + rul-predictor public repo
Streamlit Community Cloud account
streamlit_app.py starter template (with TODO markers), from FOL
rul_model.pkl, feature_cols.pkl from Lab 10
A sample one-engine CSV (sample_engine.csv) — last 30 cycles of engine #1




19.13.4 Procedure

Task 1 — Run the Streamlit app locally (40 min). The streamlit_app.py template already has the page config, cached model loading, single-engine rolling features, CSV upload, colour-coded RUL display (red < 30, orange < 60, green ≥ 60 cycles), a sensor-trend plot, and an “About this model” expander. Complete the TODOs: add your name and course to the caption; build sample_engine.csv and wire up the “Use sample data” button; fill in the “About this model” expander (your name, your actual Lab 10 RMSE, one Précitech-specific limitation). Run with streamlit run streamlit_app.py (or in Colab via pyngrok for a temporary public URL) and test a CSV upload.
Task 2 — Push to GitHub (15 min). Repo contents: streamlit_app.py, rul_model.pkl, feature_cols.pkl, requirements.txt, sample_engine.csv. Use tested pinned versions in requirements.txt (streamlit==1.39.0, scikit-learn==1.5.2, pandas==2.2.3, numpy==1.26.4, matplotlib==3.9.2, joblib==1.4.2). Push via the GitHub web UI (drag-and-drop) or the command line.
Task 3 — Deploy to Streamlit Community Cloud (20 min). At share.streamlit.io → New app → select your repo → main file streamlit_app.py → Deploy. Deployment takes 2–3 min. Common failures: rul_model.pkl > 50 MB (retrain with n_estimators=50); version conflict in requirements.txt.
Task 4 — Polish the app (30 min). Plain-language title and description a plant manager would understand; working sample-data button; complete “About this model” expander (training data = NASA C-MAPSS FD001 simulation, model = RF 100 trees / max depth 10, your validation RMSE, an explicit statement of what the model is not for); graceful handling of a wrong-column CSV.
Task 5 — Test with a classmate (15 min). Swap URLs. Try a valid CSV, an invalid CSV (wrong/extra columns, missing values), and edge cases (1-row, 1000-row). Record one bug you find in their app and one they find in yours (you need not fix them before submission).



19.13.5 Deliverables & submission

Submit via FOL: your public Streamlit URL; a screenshot of the app showing a prediction; and the public rul-predictor GitHub repository URL.



19.13.6 Rubric

Assessed against the capstone rubric in Lab 12 (Streamlit Application, 25 points; Documentation & Honest Disclosure, 15 points).



19.13.7 Instructor notes


Prep: stage streamlit_app.py and a known-good requirements.txt on FOL. Walk through one full deploy yourself the week before — Streamlit Cloud and GitHub UIs change. Confirm github.com and streamlit.io are reachable on the lab network.
Have students do the GitHub / Streamlit account creation as prep, not in the lab — it eats 20 min otherwise.
Marking: rolled into the capstone rubric; the deliverable is a URL that loads and predicts.

title: 19  Labs
section: 19.14 Lab 12 — Machine Learning, Week 6: Capstone Presentations
text:
19.14 Lab 12 — Machine Learning, Week 6: Capstone Presentations

Each student demos their deployed predictive-maintenance app live to the class and defends one technical decision — the “present to plant leadership” step of the Précitech assignment. This session carries the capstone rubric for Labs 9–12.
AI use: required across the module — but the presentation and defence must be your own.


19.14.1 Learning outcomes


Present a working technical deliverable to a non-specialist audience.
Explain and defend a modelling decision under questioning.
State the limitations of your own model honestly and specifically.




19.14.2 Prep work


Read Chapter Chapter 13, Week 6 (AI ethics in manufacturing; the broader AI landscape; where this is going).
Confirm your app loads from its public URL and the sample CSV produces a sensible prediction.
Prepare an 8–10 minute walk-through (no slides required — the app is the presentation) and be ready for 3–5 minutes of questions.




19.14.3 Materials & equipment


Computer + projector/display; internet access
Your deployed Streamlit app (public URL) and sample_engine.csv
Your Lab 10 notebook (for the RMSE / feature-importance figures if asked)




19.14.4 Procedure

Format: 8–10 minutes presenting, 3–5 minutes of questions from the class and instructor.
What to demo:

Open your app live from the public URL; show it loads and works.
Upload the sample CSV; show a prediction; explain the colour coding and how a maintenance planner would act on it.
Explain one key technical decision — engine-wise vs. row-wise split (and the RMSE you would have got the wrong way); why RUL was clipped at 125; the rolling-window size; or what the feature-importance chart shows.
State one limitation honestly and specifically (e.g. “trained on a simulation of one fault mode in one operating condition; deploying on a real engine would need retraining on actual failure data and validation against known events”).

Be ready for questions such as: what does RMSE 22 cycles mean operationally? walk through exactly what happens when a user uploads a CSV; why can’t Random Forest feature importance tell the maintenance team which physical sensor to buy? name three things needed before recommending this for deployment on the real CNC cells. “I don’t know, but I would check…” is a professional answer; guessing is not.



19.14.5 Deliverables & submission

The live presentation. No file submission — but your app URL and GitHub repo (submitted in Lab 11) must still be live and working at presentation time.



19.14.6 Rubric

Capstone evaluation rubric — Labs 9–12. The 100 points below are the marking scheme for the four capstone sessions together; how they map onto the course grade is maintained in FOL and the instructor handbook, not here.

title: 19  Labs
section: 19.15 Lab 13 — TPM/OEE, Root Cause and a New Dataset
text:
19.15 Lab 13 — TPM/OEE, Root Cause and a New Dataset

You bring the whole term together on one problem: a Précitech CNC turning cell that is not making its numbers. You compute OEE from a shift log and split the losses into the Six Big Losses; you Pareto the failure modes; you run a 5-Why and Ishikawa root-cause analysis; and then you direct an LLM to build a failure classifier on a new dataset — the AI4I 2020 Predictive Maintenance Dataset from the UCI repository (CC BY 4.0, 10 000 rows, 5 labelled failure modes). This is classification on a differently-shaped dataset, so the C-MAPSS recipe from the capstone does not carry over — the point is to show you can transfer the skill, not copy the code. Tools: Google Sheets, draw.io, Google Colab.
AI use: required for the classifier task; permitted with disclosure elsewhere. As in the ML module, you must be able to explain every line.


19.15.1 Learning outcomes

After this lab you should be able to:

Compute OEE (availability × performance × quality) from a shift log and attribute the losses to the Six Big Losses.
Build a Pareto chart of failure modes and identify the vital few.
Run a 5-Why and an Ishikawa (fishbone) analysis using measured process data as evidence.
Direct an LLM to build and evaluate a classifier on an unfamiliar, class-imbalanced dataset, and choose metrics that survive the imbalance.
Write the D4 (root cause) and D5 (corrective action) sections of an 8D report, tying model evidence back to the fishbone.




19.15.2 Prep work


Read Chapter 12 (TPM, OEE, the Six Big Losses) and Chapter 15 (troubleshooting, 5-Why, Ishikawa, the 8D report).
Skim your capstone notebook from Labs 9–12 — you reuse the workflow (load, explore, split, train, evaluate) but not the code.
Open the AI4I 2020 dataset page and confirm you can download the CSV in the browser. Columns: air temperature, process temperature, rotational speed, torque, tool wear, a machine-failure flag, and five failure-mode flags — TWF (tool wear), HDF (heat dissipation), PWF (power), OSF (overstrain), RNF (random).
Download precitech_shift_log.csv from FOL (one week of shift records for the CNC cell: planned time, downtime events, ideal cycle time, count, scrap).
Form teams of 2–3.




19.15.3 Materials & equipment


Computer with internet access
Google Sheets — OEE calculation and the Pareto chart
draw.io — the Ishikawa diagram
Google Colab — the classifier
precitech_shift_log.csv from FOL
AI4I 2020 CSV, downloaded in-browser from UCI
Chapter 12 OEE definitions and Chapter 15 8D template




19.15.4 Procedure

Task 1 — OEE and the Six Big Losses (25 min). (2 marks) From precitech_shift_log.csv, compute availability (run time ÷ planned production time), performance (ideal cycle time × total count ÷ run time) and quality (good count ÷ total count), then OEE = the product. Take each downtime and loss entry in the log and assign it to one of the Six Big Losses (breakdowns, setup & adjustment, small stops, reduced speed, startup rejects, production rejects). State which Big Loss is costing the most OEE points.
Task 2 — Pareto the failure modes (20 min). (1 mark) In the AI4I data, count how many rows carry each of TWF, HDF, PWF, OSF and RNF. Build a Pareto chart in Sheets (bars descending, cumulative line). Identify the vital few failure modes that account for most of the failures, and note where RNF sits and why that matters.
Task 3 — 5-Why and Ishikawa (25 min). (2 marks) Take the top failure mode from Task 2. Run a 5-Why chain and draw an Ishikawa diagram in draw.io with the six standard bones (machine, method, material, measurement, man, environment). Use the measured feature columns as evidence on the bones — for example, compare tool wear, torque, rotational speed and the air-vs-process temperature gap for the failing rows against the healthy rows, and put the numbers on the diagram.
Task 4 — Direct an LLM to build a failure classifier (35 min). (4 marks) In Colab, prompt an LLM to build a classifier that predicts the machine-failure flag from the five process features. You are transferring the capstone workflow, not its code — this is tabular classification, not time-series RUL regression. Report a confusion matrix and precision and recall for the failure class. The failure rate in AI4I 2020 is about 3.4 %, so accuracy is a useless metric here — a model that predicts “no failure” every time scores ~96.6 % accuracy and catches nothing. State explicitly which class-imbalance trap you hit and how you detected it. That is the lesson of this task.
Task 5 — 8D D4/D5 (15 min). (1 mark) Write the “D4 — root cause” and “D5 — permanent corrective action” sections of an 8D report for the top failure mode. Tie the model’s feature importances back to specific bones on your Task 3 fishbone, and propose a corrective action that a TPM programme could actually carry out (an autonomous-maintenance check, a setup standard, a condition limit).



19.15.5 Deliverables & submission

One team report (PDF) with: the OEE calculation and Six-Big-Losses attribution; the failure-mode Pareto chart; the 5-Why chain and the Ishikawa diagram (draw.io export) with the feature evidence on it; the Colab notebook link with the confusion matrix, precision/recall and the class-imbalance write-up; and the D4/D5 sections. Add an AI-use disclosure line. Submit on FOL by the end of the lab period.

10 marks total.

Marking: Task 4 is the point of the lab. A team that reports high accuracy and stops has missed it — full marks require them to have noticed the imbalance and switched to precision/recall (or a resampling / class-weight fix). Reused C-MAPSS code that does not fit tabular data is a red flag that the transfer did not happen.
This lab is the destination for the capstone stretch goals — see Lab 12 instructor notes.

title: 19  Labs
section: 19.16 Lab 14 — Robotic Work-Cell Design in RoboDK for Web
text:
19.16 Lab 14 — Robotic Work-Cell Design in RoboDK for Web

A take-home lab: released in week 11, due at the end of week 14, done individually, with a short screen recording as part of the submission. You design and program the Précitech kitting cell’s pick-and-place robot in RoboDK for Web — a free, no-install, in-browser robot simulator with 600+ real arms. It bookends Lab 1: toy logic in week 1, a real 6-axis industrial arm in week 14. You close the loop on the course by checking the robot’s cycle time against the takt time you computed in Lab 4.
AI use: permitted with disclosure. The station layout, the program and the cycle times must be your own work.


19.16.1 Learning outcomes

After this lab you should be able to:

Jog a 6-axis robot in joint, linear and tool coordinates and recognise singularities and joint-limit stops.
Lay out a work cell and verify that every pick and place point lies inside the robot’s reach envelope.
Program a pick-and-place cycle with targets and gripper I/O and read the simulated cycle time.
Compare a simulated cycle time against a required takt time and optimise the program to close the gap.
Compute a minimum safeguarding distance from robot stopping performance and select an appropriate safeguard.




19.16.2 Prep work


Read Chapter 8 (industrial robotics — coordinate systems, the work envelope, singularities) and Chapter 6 (machine guarding — the minimum-distance / safeguarding-distance formula and the safeguard hierarchy).
Have your Lab 4 takt calculation to hand — you need the takt time for 250 kits/day.
Open RoboDK for Web and confirm it loads and runs a sample station in your browser. No account or licence key is required.
Confirm your screen-recording tool works (the same tool the course plan’s take-home lab uses).




19.16.3 Materials & equipment


Personal computer with internet access and a browser (this is a take-home lab — no lab PC required)
RoboDK for Web — no install, no licence key
A screen-recording tool
Your Lab 4 takt time; the Précitech case study (250 kits/day, one 8-hour shift)




19.16.4 Procedure

Task 1 — Jog and observe (20 min). (1 mark) Load a 6-axis arm from the RoboDK library (any mid-size industrial arm; state which). Jog it in joint, linear and tool coordinates. Drive it toward a wrist singularity and toward a joint limit and record what the simulator does in each case. Relate this back to the teach-pendant work in Lab 1 and to the Chapter 8 coordinate systems.
Task 2 — Build the kitting cell (30 min). (2 marks) Assemble the Précitech kitting cell around the robot: an infeed conveyor delivering shaft blanks, a bearing-press station, and a tray to be filled. Place a pick point and every place point. Check that every pick and place point is inside the reach envelope; record the one reach limit that forces you to move a station, and show the before/after positions.
Task 3 — Program the pick-and-place (30 min). (3 marks) Create targets and a program that picks a blank from the conveyor, moves it to the press, then places the finished part in the tray, with gripper open/close on digital output. Run it. Record the simulated cycle time for one part.
Task 4 — Cycle time vs takt (25 min). (3 marks) Take the takt time from Lab 4 for 250 kits/day. Does one robot at your Task 3 cycle time meet takt? Then optimise — reorder targets, raise joint speeds within limits, shorten approach and retract moves — and record the improved cycle time. State by how much you beat or missed takt, and what a real cell would do if one robot could not keep up.
Task 5 — Safeguarding distance (15 min). (1 mark) Using the Chapter 6 minimum-distance formula, compute the minimum guarding distance from an assumed robot-plus-sensor stopping time (state your assumption). State which Chapter 6 safeguard you would specify for this cell (fixed guard, interlocked gate, light curtain, area scanner, two-hand control) and why.



19.16.5 Deliverables & submission

Submit on FOL by the end of week 14: a report (PDF) covering all five tasks with the reach-envelope evidence, the cycle-time and takt comparison, and the safeguarding calculation; the RoboDK station file; and a screen recording (3–5 min) showing the program running and you talking through one design decision. Add an AI-use disclosure line.



19.16.6 Rubric

10 marks total.







Deliverable
Marks




Jogging in joint / linear / tool coordinates demonstrated; singularity and joint-limit behaviour recorded
1


Kitting cell built; every pick/place point verified inside the reach envelope; the binding reach limit and the layout change recorded
2


Working pick-and-place program with targets and gripper I/O; runs in the simulator; cycle time reported
3


Cycle time compared against the Lab 4 takt; one round of optimisation with the improved time and the gap quantified
3


Minimum safeguarding distance computed from a stated stopping time; a specific Chapter 6 safeguard chosen and justified
1






19.16.7 Instructor notes


Release in week 11 alongside Lab 11, so students have the full three weeks; it is due at the end of week 14. This mirrors the course plan’s existing take-home lab pattern (released three weeks out, video submission).
Prep: the day before release, run through Tasks 1–3 in RoboDK for Web yourself on the college network — confirm web.robodk.com is reachable, the library loads, and a station can be saved and re-loaded. Have a reference station file and an expected cycle-time range (from the answer key in R/make_lab_data.R output) ready for marking.
No lab room is needed — this is done from home — but reserve 15 minutes in the week-11 lab to demo the tool and walk through the brief.
Marking: the takt comparison in Task 4 only works if the student’s Lab 4 takt was correct; if it was not, mark Task 4 on the method against a takt you supply. Watch for cycle times that are physically implausible (joint speeds cranked past limits) — that is where the “your own work” line is tested.
